utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Douglas Stringer with Matthew Olmsted, Francois Braun, and Case Manager Sebastiaan van Hooydonk for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness may be brought in. Thank you. I think the best thing to do is to keep the breaks at the same time as usual so that we don't have to think and just go on routine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rendulic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you, too. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rendulic, I remind you that you're still on your oath. Mr. Zivanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Rendulic, yesterday I asked you about the military organisation of the HDZ in the territory of Vukovar municipality and the village of Lovas. This would have started in April 1991. I'm now going to read some of the information that we have at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is tab 1 from the Defence list. It's document 2803. It should not be broadcasted or shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not going to see the document on your screen due to our Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I can't give you the source of the information. However, I'm going to read to you something from page 1, both in English and in Serbian. I'm not going to read who the participants in the meeting were. I told you when the meeting was held and where in the village of Bogdanovci. And this is what we heard: "The meeting was chaired by Tomislav Mercep. He told us at the beginning that he had received instructions from the HDZ in Osijek that we should start organising ourselves as a military organisation within the framework of the HDZ. In that the technical service should be set up and at the beginning that service will arm the most trusted members of the HDZ which will be the first recruits of the Croatian army that needs to be established in a later stage. "Tomislav Mercep appointed Josip Gazo head of this service. The military service which was also formed at the meeting was to train the armed HDZ members in handling weapons, as well as draft a war strategy for the territory of Vukovar municipality in case the creation of an independent Croatian state did not proceed peacefully. Stjepan Rados was appointed head of the service. "Vlado Rimac was appointed head of the medical service. The task of this service was to collect medical supplies and store them at certain locations in the town of Vukovar, as well as to prepare mini-hospitals or medical centres. All this had to be done illegally and in secret places because, at that time, it was illegal for the HDZ to carry out such activities placement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage the Prosecution would like to object to the form of this question which is going on quite some time. The Defence counsel is reading something into the record, something into the record that is not before this Trial Chamber, that obviously this witness has never seen or heard before. How is the witness after hearing this lengthy recitation from something going to answer a question? I think Defence counsel simply needs to put a proposition to this witness in a simplified form, in a way that the witness can answer the question. It should not be a compound, lengthy, diatribe on an issue, which is what we have now before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, may I ask -- may I add to that, without taking a position yet, that the questions you seem to want to ask the witness have already been asked and answered by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in part, Your Honour. I would just like to put the witness information in its entirety, or in this part of -- about the organisation of this military -- military organisation in Lovas. I would read him also this part of information and put him some questions related to this particular piece of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But what is -- what is the -- what is the use of giving the witness information we seem to know that he doesn't know about? Because that's already what he answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. He said that he doesn't know anything about the military organisation of HDZ. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Or medical or technical.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Right? The three components.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to put him some -- some particular information from this document related to Lovas and to ask him if he knows this piece of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If the witness may just remove his headphones, I want to discuss this particular document, and I don't believe the witness needs to hear what I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could I then ask you to remove your headphones, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution has additional concerns with regard to this particular document. We understand it to be a confession that was taken of a witness while he was under duress in detention back in 1991. The document was supplied by Defence counsel in another case before this Tribunal, and so that raises another concern about reading extensive portions of it into the record because it opens a door to a litigation of the validity of this particular document. And that is another reason we do not believe it should be read simply into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This document is provided from the Prosecution. And, as far as I know, it is on the Prosecution Rule 65 ter list. We do not have any indication that the document was provided by force or any unpermitted means. And the source of this document, I wouldn't mention it before the witness. The source of this document is also on the Prosecution list.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, every document that's on our 65 ter list is there for various reasons, not because we vouch for its reliability or anything else on it. This particular document was disclosed under our obligations under Rule 66(A), and it was put on our 65 ter list just as a convenience for the Trial Chamber and for the Defence. I think the Defence counsel knows very well where this document comes from, and I won't say anything further on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just add that we have no indication from the Prosecution to this moment that this document was provided by force or -- and -- and that's it. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, you -- you may put questions, specific questions to the witness and give him the information you need to give him in order for -- for him to answer the questions, but you should not read in those lengthy documents into the record this way. Mr. Witness, you can put your headphones on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I read out a number of names and I will repeat them today. You were familiar with all those names but one. According to our information, they implemented the decision on the military organisation of the HDZ in Lovas. Let me give you the names: Mijo Koljic, Franjo Krizmanic, Jozo Milas, Josip Grcanac, Branko Krizmanic, Marin Vidic, Josip Badanjak, Josip Filic, Ivo Madzarevic, Braco Keser. Yesterday you told us, when I asked you about Duka Filic, that that person did not exist in Lovas, or at least you didn't know about that person?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: However, yesterday, on page 1956, you spoke about somebody called Djuka Pilic or at least that's what we have on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no Djuka -- there is no Duka Filic, there is Djuka Filic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Djuka Filic exists?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Djuka Filic does exist in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What's his name?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djuka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's his real name?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Among the names I read out yesterday there was also Tomislav Rendulic. Are you two related?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we're not related. We bear the same family name, but we're not related.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned on page 1961 that, at one point in time, some anti-tank mines were delivered from Ilok to Lovas and they were then returned. I would like to ask you who was it who sent them to you?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They arrived from Ilok. I don't know who sent them. In any case, somebody brought them over from Ilok to Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was it who brought them over?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who brought them over. They arrived in the course of a night. I don't know who brought them. I already told you what transpired sometime in the month of July. They were just there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How were they transported?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By vehicles. By vehicles. You could not carry them on foot, could you? And that's how they were returned as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What vehicles? Whose vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whose vehicles those were. They arrived in the course of a night.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you present when they were returned?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was present when they were returned. I believe that the police came on the 29th of September and that's how they were returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who received them in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was on duty in the Crisis Staff on that day. Whoever it was received those mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where they were stored?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the local commune office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who guarded them?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody special. They were under lock, but it -- they were not specially guarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How come that the mines were returned to Ilok?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, they were not needed in Lovas. That's why they were under lock. And then when -- after the agreement was reached with the army to hand over all the weapons, the mines were part of that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But when you say the agreement with the army, I thought that the army wanted you to hand over your weapons to the army and those mines were not handed over to the army.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that on the 28th we handed over some of the weapons, but the army never came to collect those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 28th, you turned over the weapons you had?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you kept the mines.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the weapons. Everything remained there. The army didn't take anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't even offer them to hand over the mines.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was understood that we had to turn over everything we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From your evidence, I understood - and that's also the information I got independently - that two or three Kalashnikovs remained, some hunting weapons.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were pistols as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But nobody mentioned that there were mines, anti-tank mines.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was understood. If you're handing over one kind of weapons, you're handing over all of them. That's also included in the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you did not understand my question. What I'm putting to you - and you may answer as you see fit - what I'm saying is that, according to the information we have, and according to your evidence so far, the army was never told you had mines in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe somebody told them. In any case, they did not seek those weapons or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's also my understanding that they did not come to pick up the weapons they had been shown, those couple of Kalashnikovs and hunting rifles. However, nobody ever told them that there were anti-tank mines as well. Maybe they would have taken a different stance if they had known about the mines.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They knew about everything. Whether they wanted to take it over or not, I don't know. They knew everything that was going on in Lovas. I am absolutely sure they had all the information. As I told you yesterday, they knew when the lights were on in a particular house. There's no chance they didn't know about that. The army had very good information about what was going on in Lovas and everywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say they had information about those mines as well?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since you went to talk to the representatives of the army, when you said that Lovas has no weapons worth mentioning, nothing but those hunting rifles, a Kalashnikov here and there, or a pistol, were they able to understand from your words that you were deceiving them because you had anti-tank mines?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they understood, but they were saying there was too much of everything, which, in fact, was not true. There were just a few rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that their awareness of the anti-tank mines may have been a factor in their decision to attack Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They attacked Lovas just as any other village. They had that objective and the same scenario for every village. Sotin had nothing and was attacked. Another village also had nothing and was attacked. Tovarnik also was attacked without having any weapons. That scenario worked everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where do you get your information about the supply of arms in Sotin, Tovarnik, Ilaca, and other places?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you I went to Sotin often because my late brother, cousin, lived there. In Tovarnik and in other places, I also knew what was going on because I had my affairs through the co-operatives. And people talked what was going on. Especially when Vukovar was shelled, we knew that the war had begun. People were discussing things. They were discussing what's best to do, et cetera. I knew all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How could you know that Sotin did not have anti-tank mines as well, for instance, or Tovarnik, or Ilaca, all the other places you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can know that only from talking to people. I don't know for a fact. I claim they did not have any of these things because it was impossible for people even in bigger places in Croatia, especially in the small ones like that, to get that kind of weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about big weapons now. I'm talking about anti-tank mines specifically. They are meant to destroy tanks, APCs, et cetera. Is it your evidence that the surrounding places that you mentioned - Sotin, Tovarnik, Ilaca - did not have them?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not. Because tanks passed through Sotin, passed through Ilaca. None was ever damaged. Tanks passed by Lovas as well. Nothing ever happened. Not a single mine was used so that cannot be a pretext for attacking these villages, especially Lovas. It cannot be a pretext, an excuse for killing 68 people, civilians. And since some died of their wounds later, the total number of casualties was eventually 72.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not ask you whether the mines were ever used. I asked you whether they existed. I understood you as saying that those other places did not have the mines.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I infer you are trying to say that the army used it as a reason for attacking these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I put it as a question to you, and you are answering it the way you are answering it. I want to know how to understand your answer. Are you saying that the kind of mines that were available in Lovas were not available in other villages, or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose they did not have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I want to know, then, why those mines were given to Lovas, if they were not given to other places. Why Lovas, in particular?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably because, at that time, Lovas belonged to the Ilok area. Other villages are farther from Lovas. In terms of police work, Lovas was connected with Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You remember you gave a statement to OTP investigators. We could even look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's 2217. Tab 9. It's from 8 November 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You recall that statement?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave more than one. Now I see that it was on the 8th of November, 1995. I don't know what it was about. It was about Ljuban Devetak and this other man, Arandjelovic. But I think it was before the Zagreb District Court and this was given to investigators. Yes, now I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you first: Did you give a statement to OTP investigators only once?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was only once, but it may have been more than once. It was a long time. But it was in 1995 when we came to Zagreb as refugees. It may have been more than once.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we look at page 2 in your statement where you say that in Lovas a Crisis Staff was set up. You testified about that yesterday here. Could you first tell me, this Crisis Staff in Lovas, who was it subordinated to? Did it receive instructions from anyone? To whom did it report?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it reported to anyone. The Crisis Staff decided on its own direction and what they would do at a particular moment in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there was a Crisis Staff in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there was a Crisis Staff everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was on the Crisis Staff and who was at the head of the Crisis Staff in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Vukovar? I don't know. Apart from Mercep in Zadar, I don't know anything -- apart from Mercep and Blago Zadro, I don't know anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a connection between the Crisis Staff in Lovas and the Crisis Staff in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so because it was the same territory. It was the former municipality of Vukovar. At that time, we were still part of the municipality of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "probably," does it mean you're not sure? You are just assuming or you know it for a fact?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there was some talk about the situation in Vukovar and the topical issues, the problems that were arising. I can say, for instance, we got information from that Crisis Staff in Vukovar that a meeting was held in Pacetin of the Serbian members of the League of Communists, and one person from Lovas attended that meeting in Pacetin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You testified yesterday on page 1962 that you joined the Crisis Staff in June or May 1991.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was the end of June 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you joined the Crisis Staff at the invitation of the secretary of your co-operative, as you said.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What's that man's name?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jozo Milas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He was president or chairman of that Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He was also president of the Executive Board of the HDZ in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me now who actually set up that Crisis Staff in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The local commune and the HDZ. Because the HDZ had just won the elections, and it charted the policies in the village, and, of course, it set up the Crisis Staff, not as a political party but as the leader of the local commune, because the leaders of the local commune were members of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: About the local commune, I don't know if we were clear yesterday. We have information that the president of the local commune was Zeljko Cirba.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I told you yesterday that we have information that the leadership of the HDZ - namely, its Executive Board - implemented the decision on military organising in Lovas and set up the military medical service. You did not tell us that, but we have information about it. It's on page 2 of the document that was not broadcast or shown to the witness. In English it is on page 2, straddling page 3. It enumerates the people from Lovas who attended the meeting where the decision on military organising was made. You see, when you compare the names of those people, on one hand, and I read you some of those names yesterday, when you compare them to the names of the members of the Crisis Staff you listed in your statement, I see that it's the same group of people, apart from you. You were not present at that first meeting when the decision was made on military organising by members of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about Bogdanovci? I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I did not have occasion to read to that you passage. After Bogdanovci, after that meeting, that decision was implemented in Lovas, and also the technical, military, and medical services were established, and there was a meeting held about that in Lovas where members of the Executive Board of the HDZ adopted that decision. I've already read out the names to you. There's no need to repeat them. But when I compare that list of names and the list of names of the members of the Crisis Staff you mentioned in your statement, it's practically the same group of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you talking about the meeting in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The Prosecution objects to this line of questions. It's, again, been asked and answered. And what counsel is now suggesting is really an argument. It is not putting a question to this witness. And I repeat our concern that they are presenting information as if it is it in the record or is part of this evidence in this case. These are allegations and he simply should put a question to the witness. Did this in fact occur, are you aware that this occurred? Not saying this happened and this happened and then ask for the witness to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I just like to put to the witness that the same people who are in Crisis Staff he talked about, he spoke about in his statement, are the people who are in this document shown to the Chamber and known to the Prosecution and from -- the document from the Prosecution exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic. And what is your question about that? Was your question about those people, the members of the HDZ Executive Board being the same as the members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct. And it is -- it is in -- I -- I wanted to put the witness such coincidence between these members from the HDZ Executive Board and the Crisis Committee where he was included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But there is no question. What is the question? Or -- or ... what is the question you wanted to ask the witness about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My question was about -- my previous question was about constitution, how the Crisis Committee was constituted, how it was established. And if I have to air my further line of questions, I do it, but not before this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So ... Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think we are done with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Now, before I ask you to proceed, Mr. Zivanovic, may I remind you, as well as the witness, to pause after the questions you ask, Mr. Zivanovic, and the answer you give, Mr. Rendulic, in order to allow the interpreters to follow the course of action. Thank you. Microphone, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the information that we have, and our claim that the Crisis Staff that you testify about exist -- pre-existed your membership and that it was first established during the meeting of the HDZ board in Lovas which happened towards the end of April 1991. Do you have anything to add to that?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that a technical service was set up, as well as a medical service. There was no military organisation. They were just guards around the village. The medical service was headed by Slobodan Kacar, who was a Serb. He was also the head of the outpatient clinic and he also had a nurse, and they were the only medical service that we had. And that Slobodan Kacar was our doctor in Lovas, and he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The setting up of the Crisis Staff, could that have provoked the Serbs in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. We said yesterday that we had set up the staff to co-ordinate activities, to be the catalyst of activities in Lovas. It was supposed to inform both the Serbs and the Croats what was going on. That's why we organised that meeting with the Serbs in Mirko Lovric's house. As I already told you yesterday, at that meeting we were told that we shouldn't be afraid, that we should protect each other, and that we should endeavour to maintain normalcy in our lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How many Serbs were there in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether Djuro Prodanovic was a member of the Crisis Staff. However, Djuro Prodanovic and Milan Tepavac were always with us. They were involved in all our contacts, in all negotiations. The Crisis Staff activities were very transparent. The meetings that were held at the local commune were attended by a lot of people who were not members of the Crisis Staff, especially towards the end of that period when the situation got more compounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you didn't mention a single Serb as a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, I don't know whether Djuro Prodanovic was a member of the Crisis Staff or not. I don't know. Milan Tepavac as well. I don't know whether they were just invited guests or members of the Crisis Staff, but they were always with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You never mentioned that before.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Nobody probably asked me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would like to invite you to look at your statement. You mentioned all the people who were members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave you the names of the Croats who were members of the Crisis Staff. Nobody ever asked me about the Serbs. There's another statement of mine, talking about the meeting that was held on the 28th or the 29th which was attended by the Serbs, including Milan Tepavac and Djuro Prodanovic. That was a meeting that took place after our meeting with the army. We wanted to discuss what to do after that meeting with the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Looking at your last answer, I can see that nobody asked you about the Serbs. Are you saying that when you spoke to the investigators of this Tribunal they asked you only about the Croats who were members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you which Serbs went with us to the negotiations that took place in July. There were two Serbs there, and there was one Serb who accompanied us to Sid, and those two meetings took place in July and August. And I told you that all -- the Serbs were also with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rendulic, I never asked you that. I did not ask you who went with you to the negotiations with the JNA. I asked you who the Serb members of the HDZ Crisis Staff were. And the distinction is very clear. On the one hand, there are negotiators; on the other, there are members of the HDZ Crisis Staff. That was my question. You answered the way you could.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can also tell you that the Serbs wilfully distanced themselves from the assembly of my company. All of a sudden, they stopped taking part in the work of our organisation. When I asked them how come they didn't come to the meeting, they had all sorts of excuses. They were sick or something else. The only people who wanted to be engaged both in the Crisis Staff and in the company were Djuro Prodanovic, Milan Tepavac, and Milan Miljkovic. Those were the three Serbs who were actively involved. All the rest just distanced themselves for no reason at all, for reasons known only to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could the reason have been their information about a military organisation in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no such thing. What argument do have you to support that claim? We only had civilian village guards. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You know, we have that information, and I put it partly to you. We're familiar with that. But I know that the Serbs in Lovas knew a lot more than we do. Therefore, I believe that that -- all that information may have been very disturbing, which is why they distanced themselves and withdrew from all those bodies and activities that you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, are you giving testimony now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What -- what is your question to the witness, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question was -- my question was already put to the witness, about the -- that the Serbs were disturbed with the events in Lovas, as regards the military organisation of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And the answer was given; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned those guards around the village of Lovas. You said that they had hunting rifles. There were only two men with two hunting rifles. Is that what you said? I can tell from your facial expression that was not the case but could you please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there were several people with hunting rifles for which they had licences.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about those guards that were set up at check-points around Lovas.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were those check-points manned by two guards each?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes there were two; sometimes there were five. But those three just came to keep the other two company, to socialise with them on those check-points, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And they would spend the whole night there.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those whose turn it was to keep guard, they would come after dinner. They -- or they would bring food and drink, and they would kill time. And then when they got bored, those who didn't have to be there just went, and those who had to stay, stayed for the whole night.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: They had arms; right?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had hunting rifles or -- some of them had carbines as well. For example, as a hunter, I myself had a hunting rifle and a carbine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that those guards were set up after the incident in Borovo Selo. Could you please be more specific? How did that incident in Borovo Selo influence the setting up of the guards in Lovas? I know that there is a major difference between Borovo Selo and Lovas. In Borovo Selo, the majority population was Serb; and in Croatian [as interpreted] it was Croat; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that was a municipality, and for something like that to happen in one municipality, and for the -- for 13 police officers to be killed just like that, randomly, you can imagine how that incident reflected on the entire municipality of Vukovar. This rose a lot of concern among the population when they learned that legally appointed officers were killed in one village of their municipality, and I'm talking about the village of Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You are probably familiar with all the details. Two buses full of Croatian police officers came from Vinkovci to Borovo Selo and this resulted in an armed conflict with 13 casualties. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that there was just one bus, not two buses. However, I have to tell you this, and I have to tell the Trial Chamber something that is not part -- is not part of my statement. Already in the month of January 1991, I saw Chetniks in Borovo Selo with a friend of mine who was a Serb, Vaskrsije Vuksanovic. He asked me, in Vukovar, to take him to his brother in Borovo Selo because his brother had cancer. I took him, I drove him to Borovo Selo, to a street close to the sawmill. I left him there. He visited his brother. He returned from the house very quickly. I was in the car. And as we were leaving Borovo Selo, there is a pub on the left-hand side. Some people may be familiar with that, with that pub. I believe the name is Kod Cadje. I went to that pub together with Vaskrsije. He wanted to stand me a drink. We entered the pub and I was astonished when I saw a person with a cockade on his head, and between his legs he had an M-48 rifle and he was staring at us. I asked my friend, Vaskrsije, the Serb, he was my colleague, he was an agronomist, he was the head of the -- of a company in Tovarnik, and I asked him, What is this? And he told me, Let's have a drink and leave and then I'll tell you what this is all about. After we had that drink, we left the pub. We got into the car, and on the way to Vukovar he told me, Here, in Borovo Selo, there are about 20, if not more, of paramilitaries who had arrived. I asked him, When did they arrive? And he said, I believe that they arrived before new year. And I asked him, What are they doing here? And he said, I don't know. They arrived a day -- they imposed an obligation upon the villagers. They live at the football pitch, that is where they're stationed, and they imposed an obligation upon the villagers to feed them. Every day a couple of families have to bring them food and drinks, and I can tell you that the population is already a bit fed up with that. They're not very happy about the whole situation. And this is what he told me about that paramilitary formation that had arrived before the new year, 1991. Everybody knew about that. And now you're asking me how come we set up guards and why people in our village -- why their mind was not at rest. We had to control who was entering, both Serbs and Croats. It was simply -- as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did that friend tell you why those people were not arrested?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when the police came, they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This event you are talking about happened in January.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: January or February.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the other thing happened in May. I'm interested why were those people not arrested in the meantime. Did that friend tell you?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not tell me. The question is: Who knew about it? I don't know why they were not arrested, but they were there. I saw one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say "when the police came." Are you trying to say the police came to arrest them?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police came to free the Croat policemen who were held captive in Borovo Selo. They came with the intention of releasing them, because the paramilitaries in Borovo Selo must have taken them prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but according to my information, those two Croat policemen who came first to Borovo Selo the day before were released, unhurt.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were held prisoner, and they were later released.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And were they released?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened. But 13 policemen were killed there. I don't know when they got out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, the risk that existed in Borovo Selo did not exist in Lovas. There was no danger of a busload of Croat policemen coming only to be attacked by the locals.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But a busload of paramilitaries could have come from Sid because we were on the border with Serbia. There's only a road between us, a 5-metre-wide road. We could also fear that paramilitaries would come to Lovas, and it was quite justified to set up guards to at least check entries and exits. It was in our mutual interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what would those two guards with hunting rifles do if a busload of paramilitaries, indeed, came from Sid?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would be able to give us a sign that something was going to happen. Of course, nobody could do anything for real, just as we were unable to do anything when they organised the massacre later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But this is what I understood yesterday from you: The whole point of these check-points around Lovas manned by those guards was just to observe who was coming and going.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a stability measure, not a defence measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that the locals in Lovas were aware that those two men with hunting rifles could not stop anyone from coming in.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not even the intention, to start any fight. That's why we had no military units, no military groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that Serbs were, in fact, happy these check-points existed.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those whom I talked to were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What did those check-points give them? We now see that those check-points did not provide any effective protection. Not even from a couple of armed people, let alone a bigger military power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Gentlemen, please remind, you should pause because the interpreters can't follow. The court reporter can't follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what were they happy about?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was psychological for both ethnic groups. Anyone could come to the village, robbers, looters. Anyone. Especially after the Borovo Selo incident when all sorts of groups started roaming around.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that after the incident in Borovo Selo, a wave of violence against Serbs in Vukovar and the surrounding areas started?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware about Vukovar. I'm talking about Lovas and the villages in the Ilok area that I visited. There were no problems between Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We also have information from the same source - that's page 9 of the Serbian version; page 6, paragraph 2 of the English version - that at this meeting of representatives of the Municipal Board of HDZ Vukovar with presidents of the local branches of the HDZ and representatives of technical services, the proposal was unanimously accepted on the reorganising of the technical services into ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the last bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Into a service of internal security in local communes. According to this information, these services were tasked with monitoring and taking care of the Serbs who were deemed to be a threat to the HDZ. Do you know that something like that was organised, this internal security service in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about the meeting you refer to. I told you I was not a member of the HDZ. I know nothing at all about that meeting. And I first hear of that word, "internal security," in terms of small places like Lovas. I know that there was talk about internal security services at the level of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to our information, one group of HDZ members suggested that the houses of Serbs should be searched. Vorkapic's, Lovric's, Krnjic, Kacar, Tepavac houses.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that it was proposed, but I know that it was not done, especially the Kacar house because Dr. Kacar was the head of our medical services.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And according to this report, another group suggested that Serbs should be talked to, and I think that a meeting was organised at Mirko --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was a mixed commission formed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended the meeting. I know everything that was agreed there. There were agreements about co-existence, normal functioning, normal life in the village, without creating any problems, one for another, but I don't know about the setting up of any commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We also have information - not regarding this meeting at Mirko Lovric's house but the previous meeting I mentioned about setting up an internal security service - that it was decided that certain Serb houses be put under surveillance, and this surveillance to be done by their neighbours, their Croat neighbours. So, as a result, Franjo Mujic, Jakob Balic, Josip Balic supposed to keep the Vorkapic house under surveillance.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Perhaps that happened. Because stories were making the rounds that the JNA was coming and placing weapons in Serb houses. Whether there was any truth in that, I don't know. But the story was that a JNA truck deposited some weapons at Rado Sedlar's house. I don't know whether it's true but I know that the story was circulating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I noticed that the witness supposed that your question was: Do you know about this? But you didn't even ask. Could I ask you to put precise questions to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question was: Do you know anything about that surveillance by Croat neighbours of Serb houses?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know only what I told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, concerning what you just said, that military vehicles allegedly were bringing weapons to certain houses - let me just see the name of this man - Sedlar. The Sedlar house, for instance. Was this discussed at Crisis Staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. People talked. Not only in Lovas but in other places with a Serb population. It was said that weapons were being brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Crisis Staff make a decision about that?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff never made a decision on that issue because it was something that was just talk, in the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would a truck bringing weapons be able to easily pass the check-points unobserved?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be observed. But, as you said yourself, what could two men with hunting rifles do about it? And we also thought that we should not react to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I understood these people at the check-points were not supposed to react. They would just note that a truck passed and they would possibly inform the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the same thing I said. Their job was just to inform us what was going on. Not only about trucks but also Serbs coming from Novi Sad to visit their families. All we knew was that these people were in the village, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "we knew," you mean the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The guards reported it to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But I suppose they would also report to you that a military truck went into the village, if it had.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly would.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, according to this information we have, a number of those people we discussed before, when talking about what needs to be done, favoured the use of fire-arms and explosives without any warning against anyone who opposes that policy; whereas others allegedly said that those opponents should first be given a warning and that weapons should be used only if they resist or refuse. Was this discussed by the Crisis Staff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness -- oh, I'm sorry. But just pause before answering, please. Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just need a clarification. Defence counsel referred to "opposes that policy." I have been trying to follow this line of questioning, but I don't know what that policy is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would be more clear if I read -- read out two sentences, just two sentences. It would be very, very clear. And I would omit -- I would omit the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to this report, the method was also a matter for lively debate where some advocated the use of fire-arms and explosives without warning, while moderates - and I'm going to omit the names - said that people should be warned first. And then, if they refuse to surrender and offer resistance, weapons could be used then. The method of work for people from internal security was not decided. It was left to the individual conscience of everyone. My question is: Did you, at the Crisis Staff, hear about or discuss such decisions?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that things like that were discussed at the Crisis Staff. I don't know who the weapons should have been used against. In Lovas, everything was normal. Even the Serbs, who were less numerous than Croats, why should have anyone have used weapons against them? There was no reason. There was no need for any such debates to take place. At least this is what I know. Who was it in Lovas that we should have used arms against?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that arms were supposed to be used against some -- against some of the Serbs that lived in Lovas, but if you say that nothing -- no such thing was discussed by the Crisis Staff, then fine. According to the information that we have, the -- that some 2 kilos of explosives were brought to Lovas. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of explosives are you talking about? What do you mean when you say "2 kilos of explosives"? I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is also -- that explosive was supposed to be used for crafting explosive devices and intimidating Serbs. Do you know that in Lovas there were any attacks on the property of the Serbs and the Serbs themselves?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can corroborate that by an analysis. When paramilitaries entered Lovas, and when they interrogated people in Lovas - and I'm talking about their police - they called a friend of mine who is now deceased. I'm sure that you will find it in their records. When they asked him - Ivica, Ivica Sabljak - Can you tell us what the Croats wanted to do to the Serbs in Lovas? And I answered them, he says, Have any of the window-panes on any of the Serbs' houses broken? And Ivica says, No. The one who interrogated him was Milan Devcic. He said, Let him go, let him go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I refer to page 2 and -- page 3 -- page 2, paragraph 1, of the English version of the first document, document -- which is not shown to the witness or -- and broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm a little bit confused, Mr. Zivanovic. Do you intend to tender that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Just that you could follow -- follow what part of document I refer to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And one more question, but the witness should perhaps take his head -- headphones off for just one moment. Please, Mr. Rendulic. Could you take your headphones off? You're referring, Mr. Zivanovic, to this document as a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Twice you said "this report." So what is it exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is -- it is a statement. And because of that, I did not ask to be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just mention that we are also concerned about that word of "report" because it seems to lend some credibility to the document. And when you present to a witness, We have a report, that says this, the witness has never seen the report, doesn't know who issued the report, they're going to be in a position where they feel like they are somehow having to explain away a report that might be official or might not be. Our position has always been just put the question to him without referring to a report or to a statement or anything else. You can simply say, Were you aware of 2 kilograms of explosives? And if he says no, move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, in the B/C/S I mentioned "document." I don't know if it is translated as "report." It is not report. It is actually a statement. And refer to the pages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So could I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- so that my friends from the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber could see what I refer to. It is only purpose why I refer to some pages of this document which is really very [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you to -- in your next questions, to refer to -- only refer to information we have. Would that be okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Mr. Rendulic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rendulic, do you know that an explosive device was thrown into the courtyard of the Devcic family?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I refer to the transcript page 1669 through 1670, and 1682 to 1683.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I heard that. But that Bozo Devcic is not a Serb. He's a Croat. It was a Croat house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What about Milan Devcic?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Devcic was his son.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if he was perhaps responsible for some crimes committed in Lovas? I'm talking about the son.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Milan Devcic was convicted in Belgrade earlier this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was tried as a member of a military or a paramilitary formation set up on the Serbian side or perhaps on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was tried as a member of a paramilitary Serb unit. However, he was previously a member of the Croatian police. He left the Croatian police, and like everybody else, he went in search for a new job. At the time when all that was happening, when this whole thing involving the explosives was happening, nobody knew where Milan Devcic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean when that explosive was thrown into his father's house?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nobody knew whether he was still on the Croatian side or whether he crossed over to another side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a farm belonging to Dobrivoje Katanski was also blown up?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not in Lovas. That was outside of Lovas in Jelas forest. That Katanski was not a villager of Lovas. He actually resided in Belgrade full time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that the fact that he resided in Belgrade was not a reason to blow up his farm.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the house belonging to Ljubisa Todorovic was first looted and then set on fire?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that it was looted or set on fire. I was on good terms with Ljubisa. Ljubisa had enjoyed a very decent and normal treatment in Lovas. A year ago, the two of us attended the same wedding. He never complained about anything. He never told me anything to that effect. He never told me that his house was looted. I simply cannot believe that it was, that anybody would have done that, that it would have occurred to anybody to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say that it was not looted. Or are you saying that it was neither looted nor set on fire?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that it was looted. I'm sure that it was not looted. I don't know whether it was set on fire or not. I -- I can't be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the house belonging to Milorad Novakovic? Was that house looted and set on fire?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milorad Novakovic. Milorad Novakovic was an employee of my company at that time and he still is. He lived with his parents. I'm trying to reconstruct the situation. That house was never touched. His brother still lives in that house, and Milorad lives in another house. I really wouldn't know. Both his brother and himself still live in Lovas, and they were both employees of my company until his brother got sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Rajko Lovric's house? Was that house looted and set on fire?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to laugh. Rajko Lovric's house is still intact. His house is still in the centre of the village. The municipality purchased his house in order to replace it by a new building. But the house is still there. Now you can see how many erroneous information circulate around. You can come to Lovas. You will see that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that that house was never looted or are you saying that it was not set on fire?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not looted or set on fire. I've told you. Come to Lovas. You will see it for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, when I am looking at the instance of throwing an explosive into the courtyard of Milan Devcic's father's house and the setting on fire of Dobrivoje Katanski's farm, you say about Ljubisa Todorovic that you are not sure whether his house was set on fire or not. Can you tell us, when you spoke to a colonel whose name was Zelimir Petrovic in the month of September, did you have an impression that he believed you when you said that the situation in Lovas was calm?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you think that the army was aware of those incidents?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. They heard a lot of things, so I suppose that they were aware of those things as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, on that occasion, you did not mention those incidents that had occurred in Lovas; right?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I must tell you that if, indeed, those incidents did happen, the military would have known about that. They would have asked us about those things because they asked us about more banal things, and they didn't ask us about those incidents. Maybe that -- if those incidents did happen, maybe they occurred after our conversation with the army, after the month of October, because if they had happened before, I'm sure that the representatives of the army would have inquired about those incidents. And they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now tell me, please, you said that some of these incidents did actually happen. And now from your previous answer, I understand that you said that if those incidents had happened in the first place. Can we be more specific? Let's start with the three incidents that I've just mentioned. Are you saying that they did happen? For example, that incident involving the courtyard of Milan Devcic's father. Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did hear about that, that an explosive device was thrown into that courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And then when we mentioned Dobrivoje Katanski, as far as I understood you, you said that his farm was indeed blown up; right?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that happened. But I don't know when and whether the military knew about that incident when we talked to them. If that happened prior to that meeting, the military would have inquired about that incident because they inquired about more banal things than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe they didn't want to ask you about that because they were putting your sincerity at test.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what they were doing and what they wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Speculation, calling for speculation, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When did you learn that Milan Devcic was involved in the Serb military formations?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt about that when I went to Sid for negotiations. I bumped into him. He was a member of those paramilitary units in Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody knew about that in Lovas before that?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. We could only speculate, like we did about everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you say that you cannot rule out the possibility that that explosive device was thrown into his father's house after the talks that you had with Colonel Zelimir Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I don't know. I don't know when that happened. I don't know who did it. There were a lot of speculations. Maybe it was just a provocation, and that provocation could have come both from the Serbian as well as from the Croatian side. It's just a speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, i would change the topic and maybe it is time for a break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Witness, Mr. Rendulic, we'll take the first break. Come back at 11.00. You will be escorted out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Rendulic, we also have information that in July/August 1990 at a meeting of HDZ presidents and those three services I've already mentioned, a decision was made to establish volunteer detachments, and a decision was made to form platoons within those detachments. Do you know anything about the setting up of volunteer detachments and those platoons?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about volunteer detachments or platoons. I know what I said about guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We also have information that a volunteer detachment of 120 men was formed in Lovas, commanded by Markica Grcanac.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's completely inaccurate. Because that Markica Grcanac would not have been able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there was some sort of review held of a volunteer detachment from Lovas in the presence of about 50 people and all members of the board of the HDZ in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have heard about it. And there are other people who would know better than I.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked again to not start answering before the question is over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the interpreters ask once again to pause after Mr. Zivanovic's question. I know it's difficult, so I remind you from time to time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. But I jump ahead of myself and get carried away and hasten to answer. Thank you for this reminder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that some kind of review was held of volunteer detachments in Bogdanovci village involving a volunteer detachment from Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about Bogdanovci. Because, I tell you, I was not part of these units and I know very little about what went on in Bogdanovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information we have - that's transcript page 1674, lines 2 through 4 - it was broadcast on TV.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you know nothing about volunteer detachments and the detachments -- sorry, platoons within those detachments?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, I know only about civilian guards around the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You probably remember that you testified before the Higher Court in Belgrade - the War Crimes Chamber - in the Lovas case. That was on the 25th of February, 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see 1D148, please. It's tab 4, I think. [Interpretation] Could we move to page 75 in B/C/S and page 69 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were asked by counsel, Gradimir Nalic, and you answer: In Lovas there was a Crisis Staff and then those platoons on duty were organised. Those platoons were made up of civilian population. Counsel: How many men in one platoon? Answer: I don't know depends on the platoon. 10 to 15, depending on how people joined. You remember this evidence you gave?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. You didn't read where Gradimir Nalic says: How many platoons were needed in one shift to guard the village? I maybe mentioned platoons, but only platoons guarding the village, not the kind of unit that you mention. This was something Nalic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What are these platoons that guarded the village?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you. We had to have a roster for this guard duty so that everyone should know when they are on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, they were organised into platoons.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Squads, platoons, I don't know. But we had to have a schedule, a roster. Who goes on guard when. And Nalic asked how many of these platoons were needed to guard the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, he asks you: Do you know, in view of the organisation, the chain of command, how was it organised below you? Was it organised into platoons, companies, squads in your village? And then you answer how each community organised themselves, and then you speak about Lovas.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- you see, it says here: "We did not stand guard in platoons. We stood guard by check-point." That's my answer to this counsel who was questioning me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, platoons existed.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Platoons, or squads, I really don't know. We called them platoons because we know what a platoon means. We had done our military service in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You have said that the co-operative, while you were the general manager, gave loans to its co-operants. And we have information that the agricultural co-operative in Lovas made a certain number of loans in cash to a number of HDZ members who were simultaneously members of volunteer detachments. And these loans were, in fact, made for the purpose of purchasing weapons. Do you know anything about this borrowing -- this lending?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No loans were ever given specifically to buy weapons. In its business with co-operants from Opatovac, Lovas, even Tovarnik, the co-operative provided loans much earlier and continued in 1991 for production, livestock breeding and farming. We also gave loans to some of our co-operants for other purposes. When telephone lines were being built, we provided loans of 1200 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You don't have to describe all the things you financed. Concentrate on my question. According to the information we have, these loans were officially made for the purchase of agricultural inputs or livestock, but that money, because these were cash loans, were used to buy weapons.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that were true, there would have been much more weapons. Yes, there was an increased demand for cash loans at that time, and we only later found out why. People were speculating, making profit. The inflation was high, so people went to Serbia and Bosnia, bought German marks, returned to Croatia, and within 10, 15 days, they would have made 10, 15 per cent profit on the foreign exchange differentials. But we never gave anything for the purchase of weapons. Whether anybody bought weapons, I really don't know. May I just add. That man you mentioned yesterday, Ivo Madzarevic, you refer to him as some technical service for supplying weapons. Before our talks with the army, he bought a hunting rifle in Sid. I asked him about it, and he said, Yes, all this commotion will pass, and I will still have my hunting rifle for hunting purposes. That's how weapons were bought, because had you to obtain a licence first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, you don't know if any of those who got cash loans used them to buy weapons later or not. That's how I understood your answer here.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if -- excuse me, may I? If there had been mass purchase of weapons, then there would have been many more weapons at the time when we were supposed to turn them over.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My information is that it involved 15 to 20 such loans, and they amounted to 6- to 7.000 dinars. But if you don't remember those details, tell me.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the amount. I said loans were provided much earlier, and we still provide them, cash loans for production purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Jozo Milas and Josip Grcanac collected foreign currency in Lovas to buy weapons again? That's our information.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You say they could have bought them using those loans. Then why would they go around begging?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If only a certain number of loans was given, obviously other people did not apply for them or did not qualify for them. I'm asking you, independently of loans, do you know that these two people, Milas and Grcanac, collected money from citizens, foreign currency to buy weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to repeat his answer. He started it again too early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you repeat your answer, please. Mr. Witness -- just -- just one moment. You can see when you should start talking. That is, when, on the screen, the typing stops. That means that the interpreter has finished and the court recorder has finished. So that could be helpful for you. So could you now repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'm an operative. I have never been before courts much, and in operative work you have to be quick. I said I don't believe Milas and Grcanac collected that money because they didn't need to. If there were loans, as you say, why would they go around begging to buy weapons? Milas worked in our company and Grcanac worked in Vukovar. I don't know where would they find the time to go around collecting money to buy weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, Mr. Rendulic, this was a really simple yes-or-no question. I mean, a question you could answer with: Yes, I know that they did, or yes, I do not know that they did. And obviously you don't know -- you -- you don't know about it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
