utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that sometime between the 10th and 15th of September, 1991, weapons were distributed in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that weapons were distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to our information, 20 Kalashnikovs were delivered to Lovas at that time.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I must say something. If things had been purchased with the help of loans and if those had been delivered to Lovas, how many weapons would have ended up in Lovas? A lot, I suppose. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you don't know anything about the delivery of the 20 Kalashnikovs to Lovas in the month of September 1991?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, and I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now, tell me, please, you know that the Serbian Democratic Party existed in Croatia at that time. Were there any members of that party in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't know that there was a Serbian Democratic Party, and I didn't know who its members were. I'm not aware of its existence in Lovas either. Are you talking about the SDS, the so-called SDS?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You really don't know that that party existed in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that it existed in Croatia, but I didn't know that it existed in our area, in our region.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, as part of your testimony, you said that there was no police in Lovas, on pages 1951 to 1954. Let's look at the same exhibit that is on the screen. Page 70 in B/C/S; and pages 63 and 64 in English. Again, Attorney Gradimir Nalic asked you this: "Tell me, please, how did it happen that the temporary Ilok MUP police station ... was there, was it not ... in a school? "Witness Adam Rendulic: Because we asked for it ... we were quite insecure. We had nothing to defend ourselves with. We saw what was going on, that those military and paramilitary troops were constantly passing through, and actually the population was alarmed and fled. And so in order to alleviate the pressure on Ilok, they too asked for a branch to be established there so that the people would feel more secure." The next question: "... what duties did they perform, this branch with 10 to 15 men ... in the village? They did not simply sit in the school, I presume." And you said: "Well, they did not. They patrolled the village." And later on you say that they drove around in civilian vehicles and that they wore chequer-board signs on their uniforms. Yesterday you testified that there were no police in Lovas itself, but, rather, that the police officers from Lovas would go to Tovarnik and some other places where they worked. My impression is that what you stated in front of the Higher Court in Belgrade contradicts your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. But you have to put that in time. Yesterday we talked about two different time-periods. The early one, after the events in Borovo Selo, in May; and these particular policemen arrived towards the end of September at a time when we negotiated with the army. We requested for a police detachment to be sent to Lovas to provide the villagers with a higher level of security. We wanted to make sure that the arrival of the army would not cause unexpected events and to prevent the locals of Lovas from fleeing to Ilok. I told you yesterday that a lot of the population, after our negotiations on the 28th, left and went to Ilok. That's why we asked for the policemen to come. They were billeted in the school because the school was closed, and those police officers stayed for a few days and then they returned to Ilok, from which they had come from in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, could we have a precise reference of -- from the transcript where the witness would have said that there were no policemen from Ilok coming to Lovas but going to other places. Because in -- in this -- here -- here, the witness seems to have said that they patrolled Lovas. Didn't the witness say the same, in other words, yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday he said there was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Precise reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I said yesterday, precise reference, pages 1951 through 1954. He said that there was no police which was in -- in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Which was stationed in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was no station in Lovas. There was no standing police in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Does he say the contrary in this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understood it that they stayed in a school -- in the school in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: His answer is: Well, they did not. They patrolled the village. Nothing else. And you read the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is a question -- I'll read it in the B/C/S. [Interpretation] Tell me, please, how come that the Ilok police found themselves in the -- in a school? Are you referring to the Lovas school? "Because we wanted them to come. We did not feel safe."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday you did not talk about the year 1991. You talked about the year 1990; right?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's take things slowly. Yesterday we talked about the year 1991. However, prior to our talks with the army which took place in September. Up to then, there were no police in Lovas. I had just told you, and I don't want to go over the same grounds again, we invited the police to come after our talks with the army, and I told you why we did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After the contacts with the army, after your initial contacts, and after you invited the police, after the police arrived, did you inform the army that you had requested the Ilok police to come to Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously you did not understand me. I told you that the police was invited after our talks with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My impression was that you had several rounds of talks with the military in September 1991, that you did not have just one round of talks.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked on two occasions, on two different days: On the 27th, and on the 28th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And after that second day, after the 28th, you invited the Ilok police to come to Lovas; right?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now let's look at the part which concerns the attack on Lovas. I would like to ask you something in very general terms. Since you served in the army, you should know this. Could you distinguish between a regular recruit and a member of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not easy, but, yes, you could distinguish between the two. Mainly by behaviour and by appearance. Regular recruits, soldiers, were more controlled and better groomed, whereas the members of the Territorial Defence were a bit more unruly, and in terms of their appearance they were not young lads. They were mostly middle-aged men, so one could conclude that they belonged to paramilitaries rather than to the regular military.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I told you that members of the JNA serving their compulsory service looked better groomed, that they -- they were clean-shaven, that their haircut was neater, in comparison with the others?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly what I meant and what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to talk about the prior shelling of Lovas. I will go straight to the 10th October 1991, i.e., to the time when the attack was carried out and when the JNA entered Lovas. At that time, you were in your house. You were hiding until noon or thereabouts, and then you left your house, if I understood you properly. You said that there was no armed resistance put up against that attack on Lovas. Could you please explain how you knew that, seeing that you were in your cellar? How could you know what was happening outside and around the village?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason I know that was that a prior agreement had been reached that -- that after the Sid talks, we realised that we did not have the strength to resist the army and that we should not do it at all, and that was generally accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the agreement prior to the attack. However, my question was different. Are you claiming that there were no skirmishes, that there were no armed conflicts, or whether there was just an agreement that those should not happen?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that there were no armed conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see 1D168. It is tab 8. 161, sorry. Tab 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, this should be something that's not shown to the witness but simply put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, yeah. That's correct, it should not be broadcasted or shown to the witness. [Interpretation] I'm looking for the second page in B/C/S; and in the English version, it is the last paragraph on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a report that we obtained, and I'm going to read a paragraph from it. "Fighting for our village, Lovas, lasted several hours, four to five hours all together. The resistance and the defence was put up by members of the ZNG, among whom there were also our own locals, i.e., they were all locals of Lovas. And all those who fought, i.e., who defended the village, withdrew towards Ilok. Those of us who did not participate in the fighting, we were all civilians, the elderly, women, and children, remained in the village." This is a piece of information that we have from which you can conclude that there was fighting around the village and that, after four or five hours, the fighting stopped and defenders withdrew. Can you comment?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to control myself and help the work of the interpreters. I had to laugh. Again, this is incorrect, and this is not truthful, like so many things before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How can you know that from the point of view of your cellar where you were hiding?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in the cellar all that time. We were all, or most of us, in one place. I told you yesterday, we were at Badnjara [phoen], all those who went to Ilok later on. The women, the children, mostly civilians, and none of the defenders or those who participated in fighting were in Lovas. I apologise. Even the Crisis Staff that we discussed and the HDZ members had not been in Lovas for three or four days prior to that. They had left for Ilok even before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say they left for Ilok. Does that mean that was before the attack on the 10th of October?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion once you left Lovas to meet at least once for -- with Jakov Balic, for instance?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only Jakov Balic, but also with some other men who had gone out with their hunting rifles and pistols. They were in my sector, some 200 metres away, while I was in the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was Tomo Balic one of them? Was he amongst them?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tomo Balic, he was in Vukovar. He wasn't even in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What about Sinisa Pavlicic?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sinisa Pavlicic at the time was just a young lad. He was a kid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What about Josip Conjar?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for Josip, I can't really remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, we have information that they had all taken part in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I refer to the page, transcript page 1755, lines 15 through 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like you to tell us one more thing to do with the funeral in Sotin that you mention, the funeral of a relative of yours. You told us that he was a civilian, in fact. Please just reply --

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So he was not a member of any military formation or the police or the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were just part of the patrols or guard details at the check-points, like Milo and Vaso.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you said that he was killed in the fighting in Borovo Naselje. I believe this was the engineers' club or so, in that building or around that building. Did anyone explain to you why it was that in order to defend this building in Borovo Naselje, he was called to come, he was asked to come from Sotin, and get there as a civilian?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why he was called up but he was not the only one who left. From that check-point where they were, and this was in the direction of Vukovar, the check-point on the road, they were asked to come and assist at the technical club, or technological club, in Borovo Naselje in order to help to push out the paramilitary forces or, as they referred to them, Chetniks, from that building towards Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there enough men in Borovo Naselje itself to resolve that problem so that your relative, for instance, as a civilian, had to be called up to take part in the defence? Weren't there enough police and ZNG members there?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that he was not the only one who went there. There were ten or 12 of them who left the check-point, the check-point towards Vukovar, and this engineers' club belonged to Vukovar town, and we know how few defenders there were in Vukovar at the time to defend the entire area of both Vukovar and Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The group that your relative was in who left, they were all civilians; right?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And they were armed?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, some of them had -- they had various, different weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that many local people in Lovas had weapons and that they had permits for those weapons. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that misstates his testimony. I think he stated that about 30 to 35 people had weapons, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that of some 30 to 35 people; right? Was that your assessment, or did you know exactly how many men had permits to carry weapons?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I was a hunter myself and -- I was able to learn that information from the sports club that I was a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There were also pistols, if I'm not mistaken. So this was not your standard hunting weapon, was it?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously, you're not familiar with these things. Each hunter has a permit for side-arms in order to fire that shot of mercy, the mercy shot, so I, too, had a pistol as a hunter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You are aware of these 30 to 35 permits that were issued to the members of the hunting club; correct? Now, do you know whether the Ministry of Interior in Vukovar issued permits to people who are not hunters?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know anything about that, but it was possible to obtain a weapon, to request a permit, and once it was assessed that they were entitled to it, then the permit would be issued to such a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said on page 1981 that the military knew about the permits issued by the police. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why is it that you thought that the army would know about the permits issued by MUP in Vukovar? Permits to carry weapons.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we knew because a number of policemen who worked in Vukovar, most of them Serbs, knew this, and they checked the files to see who had weapons and who didn't. And, on the other hand, a lot of people bought hunting weapons in Sid. That's where I got my weapon. There was a company called Jelen. So, more or less, we all went to Sid to buy weapons, which is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you believed that the Serbs who worked -- who were employed at the Vukovar MUP provided information to the military through unofficial channels about the number of permits issued and to whom they were issued.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could put it that way, but it was no secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was not a secret to whom?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to anyone. People publicly carried their weapons, and you could see in public when they went hunting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you believed that the army could know about this because people knew generally who it was who had weapons and then they would report this to the -- to the army, information of that nature?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you talked about the circumstances in which volunteer Djordjevic was killed. He took part in the operation in Lovas on the 10th of October. So I would like to ask you - because you were not present yourself - where you got the information how all of this transpired?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived in Ilok, of course, we exchanged information about everything that had happened and how it went, and that's when I learned about this paramilitary and how he got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can't you tell us who you got this information from?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really tell you specifically because this happened on the -- on the way out of the village towards Opatovac, so it wasn't in the village itself that it happened. And, there, I was told, during the talks with the army, when they told me, Well, we can't control what's going on in the fields, we can only keep under control what was happening in the village. And now to point out specifically who it was who told me that, I can't really recall because there were a lot of us who had fled to Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you told the army that you could not guarantee for events outside the village in the fields, what was it that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, around Lovas there were fields, cornfields and vineyards and so on, so all these things could have happened some 100 or 150 metres away from the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But the defence of Lovas then would not be organised within the houses themselves, but, rather, outside of the village itself - at least that's my understanding - because it would -- one could infer from this that the defence would not be put up from the houses themselves but, rather, from the villages that were around -- from the fields that were around the village.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zivanovic, I know what your task is, but I've already said that there was no defence. The defence had just fallen apart on the 29th of September, when we had those talks with the military. We knew that there was no chance of putting up any resistance. There were no check-points anymore. Nothing. Everyone had already left. And there was nothing left around the villages anymore. Because, had it been so, had there been checks, the paramilitaries wouldn't have been able to reach -- to come close -- to come up close to the village during the night. Because when the artillery attack was over, they moved from the very houses on the outskirts of the village. So had there been some guards overnight, they would have been able to see this, and then they could shoot in the air to let us know that there were paramilitaries there, that they were already in those Serb houses. And, of course, in that case, people would have fled during the night and not have been caught in their sleep, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would just like to clarify one thing here. When you said to the representatives of the JNA that we couldn't guarantee for what was going to happen outside the village in the fields, that should be taken as you being unable -- you being unable to guarantee there would be no resistance in the villages. I'm not saying that that's what happened, but I'm just saying when you said to the representatives of the JNA, We guarantee that there won't be any resistance from the village but we can't provide the same guarantees for the meadows around the village, then that could be understood as -- that there would be resistance around the village from the fields; correct? So I'm not talking about what happened on -- on the day of the 10th of October itself.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, this is -- you're putting something I didn't say to me. We were not talking about resistance. We were talking about possible incidents from the time when there were these negotiations going on because we knew that there could be incidents on the border itself and then the army would have an excuse to intervene. But we never talked about any resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that yesterday you mentioned the name of this man who was wounded and who then fired his pistol and shot the volunteer Djordjevic. The name was not recorded in the transcript so could you please repeat it now.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned Antun Sabljak, whose nickname was Rodjo. He was the first man who was killed, but this was outside of the village when he tried to flee in his car. I also said that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was looking at this list shown you by the Prosecutor yesterday, the people who were killed on the 10th of October, and I didn't find his name. I'll try to find it. I don't have much time left.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I don't have the exhibit number, but the 65 ter number is 5062. And perhaps I can speed this whole process up by referring Defence counsel to number 16 on that list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit Number P315, admitted under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: 15, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Will we have it on the screen? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is page 3, as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And please look ... Could we just zoom in on the list. I don't see Antun Sabljak on this list, among the victims, casualties. At any rate, I won't dwell on this list anymore. I wanted to clear up just a few more matters with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, shouldn't we give the witness the opportunity to check the list and say whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- it's there or not [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have looked at the list, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where? My screen is off. Tomo Sabljak is the name. We called him Antun. It's under 17, Tomo Sabljak. But I don't think this is right. I think his name is Antun Sabljak, nicknamed Rodjo. You can check and you will find his name on all the lists of casualties from Lovas. The person who made this list made a mistake. His name is Antun and they abbreviated it to Tomo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, the name Antun Sabljak is not on the list, is it? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's that person. I'm sure. And it's verifiable on all lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We should like to at P320. These are referendum results for Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You've said you don't believe that there were two factions in Ilok, after seeing a video, and you can see it from these results. It's on page 2018 of the transcript. When you look at these results, it turns out that 260 people turned out for the referendum out of the total indicated here -- sorry. Out of the total of 5600, 2.684 turned out. 940 voted for, and 2.619 voted against. I would say that there were, in fact, two groups of citizens.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where do you see who voted for? I see that the number of ballots indicating against is 2.500-something. Where do you see for?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not very legible here but in the translation you can see the number 240 voted for.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Doesn't this tell you that there were, indeed, two groups of citizens. One was against the proposal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, for and against what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I tried to -- I try to clarify it with the witness. [Interpretation] Could we now look at P319.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, there are two questions posed at the referendum. One was: Are you in favour of surrendering the totality of weapons and signing an agreement with the JNA? And the second question is: Are you in favour of collectively moving out in view of the situation? To be quite honest, I don't know whether the results that I showed you before were for the first, or the second, or for both questions together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zivanovic, you're turning back to your yesterday's question about the two factions, on the basis of this; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But if I remember this well, your question yesterday about two factions was about one faction being in favour of putting up resistance; and the other faction being against that. Is my memory correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that it was related to Ilok. I -- I don't know ... maybe -- maybe I am wrong. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So what -- what exactly is your question about the two factions? Two factions --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is that -- my question is if he -- sees the results of the referendum, could he draw the conclusion that there were two factions of citizens in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: With regard to the question whether to surrender arms and whether to move out of Ilok?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what was the result of what question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: One of those two?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Not about putting up resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. It was not the question in the referendum. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. President, I share your confusion because the video we showed yesterday, that was the issue that was brought up by Mr. Hadzic, whether they would surrender or not. And so I understand the confusion. But if the issue is only whether some people voted for surrendering their arms and others voted for leaving, that's -- we have no problem with that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So, my question is just this: I really don't know which of these two questions featured at the referendum. But in any case, don't you see from the results that there were two groups of citizens? One group of citizens was in favour; the other was against. Whatever the question was.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. First of all, not everyone turned out for the referendum, as these things usually happen. Second, not all Croats moved out of Lovas. Some stayed. The same thing happened in Ilok. Some wanted to move out of their homes, and some wanted to stay. And most of the people who stayed were Slovaks. But you cannot talk about separate factions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question concerns the evidence you gave yesterday; namely, that, on the road leading out of Ilok, some people had seen Slavko Dokmanovic. I've gone through your previous statements given to the OTP, and before the District Court in Zagreb in 2003, and your testimony before the Higher Court for War Crimes, and I noticed you never mentioned that before.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. Nobody asked me about it. And I believed it wasn't important because -- but I would have liked to have seen him because we knew each other well. Of course, he is dead now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rendulic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I did check my memory on the two faction issue, and I refer you to page 75 of the yesterday's transcript, where you asked: "He mentions that: 'In Ilok, one wing offered to surrender while the other extreme wing will not allow it.' Were there two wings or factions ..." And in the next question you say: "Was there any faction that was in favour of armed conflict or of entering into armed resistance against the JNA?" So that's quite a different question about factions than the one you put to the witness today. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Olmsted, I suppose after the break you will have re-direct questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very limited, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Witness, we'll take the second break now. We come back at 12.45. You will be escorted out of the courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Rendulic, I have a few questions to clarify some issues that came up during your cross-examination. I promise I'll try to be quick so you can finish with your testimony very soon. The issue of loans was raised by the Defence today. You were asked a number of questions about loans that the Lovas co-operative would give to the community. Can you tell us, when a person received a loan from the co-operative, did they have to provide proof that they were going -- they used the money for the purposes that the loan was provided?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not a single loan was provided without a contract, and the contract stipulated for what purpose the loan is given, and any producer that benefitted from a loan had to repay in kind. If it was given for livestock, for farming, they would repay in kind. Only in exceptional cases did they repay in money.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And in 1990 and 1991, was there any problem with this issue? Were people using their funds for purposes that were outside the agreement, or were they able to establish that they used it for the proper purpose of the loan?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they did not use loans for other purposes, and people could not repay in kind because of the war that began in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Why did the co-operative continue to provide loans in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we kept lending as long as we were able to continue operating. When the war began, the co-operative ceased to be active, and that included a cessation of lending, and the entire operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when you said "when the war began, the co-operative ceased to be active," when was that? What month?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the way up to the 1st of October we thought and hoped that nothing much would happen. There would be no war. The whole situation would calm down and that the things that later happened would not. By the time I left, there was no work going on in the co-operative or in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Had you known that Lovas would be attacked by the JNA or other Serb forces, would the co-operative have continued to provide loans up until October?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we had known, of course, we wouldn't. We would have saved the money or transferred it somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, yesterday at transcript page 2031, you mentioned that a ZNG unit was located at the Vupik farm. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you tell us, where was that Vupik farm located?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The headquarters was in Vukovar. And this was a local branch in the municipality of Opatovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So the Vupik farm that had a ZNG unit at that time was in Opatovac?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Opatovci.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Opatovac, correction. Opatovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Now, if you know, how long was this ZNG unit at that location? For what period?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very briefly. I think I said yesterday that there was an air attack on that area, and luckily that unit had left before the attack. That must mean that they were gone by July, mid-July.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, today you were asked a number of questions about the police who came from Ilok at the end of September of 1991 to help patrol, maintain peace in the village of Lovas. Can you tell us, first of all, how many police came from Ilok at that time?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was ten to 15 policemen, but not to maintain law and order. There was law and order. We invited them so that if paramilitaries or the army come, they should protect us and give moral support to the population so it doesn't flee to Ilok. At that time, we still had peace and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were they brought to fight the JNA if they came into the village?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would ten people stand up to them? There was never any mention of any forces in Lovas, civilian guards, or those ten policemen opposing the army that far outnumbered anything we could muster. And I saw that with my own eyes when I went for talks in Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned today that they left a few days after they arrived and returned to Ilok. Can you tell us, did they leave before or after the shelling began in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Long before the attack. They returned because they said themselves: What are we doing here? We can't stand up to the army. Part of the population of Lovas had already left. It's peaceful here. We have no business here. And it -- I talked to them myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Today the Defence counsel put to you that you were in your cellar the whole time on the morning of the 10th of October, and you clarified that you were, in fact, not in your cellar the whole time that morning. Can you tell us, whether you were in your cellar or outside your cellar, were you able to observe what was going on in your neighbourhood on the 10th of October?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the first shells started falling around 7.20, I was in my cellar. But when the shelling stopped, I went outside. My neighbour called me and said, Adam, come and see my -- the grandfather died. Milan Latas; I mentioned him before. And then my father came. We started talking about what we were going to do. Unfortunately my father was also killed later. I said, I don't know. Let's go back inside. Perhaps there would be more shelling. Such provocations happened before and then this woman said --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. -- yes. I'm sorry. I don't mean to interrupt you but I just want to finish up very quickly here. I just was asking you whether -- wherever you were that morning, were you able to observe what was going on in your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was able to see from the door of the cellar of my father-in-law. I was looking for a moment to run away. I had already gone outside and then returned. And my neighbour said, There's shooting from all sides. And those were these dum-dum bullets that were very loud. We saw all kinds of military uniforms, green and camouflage, and even people in workers' overalls.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And while you were inside or outside, did you see any armed resistance by the Croat citizens of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said this to the opposing counsel. There was no resistance. Resistance was impossible. General panic prevailed after the shelling, and even those at the Crisis Staff who said that we had our own territorial units formed, they themselves fled a few days later. That's why we formed that body to calm the situation down, to calm the citizens, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: On the morning of the 10th of October, where were the Croat citizens who were still in Lovas that morning? Where were they during this attack?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the population - it was 7.20 - people were still inside their homes. The children were still in bed. There was no -- not much work going on those days, so people mostly stayed at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when the attack -- attack began, did they remain in their homes?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they scattered. Each to a different side. They were all over the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you testified that you were in your cellar. Were you -- were other citizens in their cellars as well?

utterances.speaker: ADAM RENDULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who had cellars, they were in the cellars. My neighbour of whom I spoke yesterday, the lady with two young children, she did not have a cellar. That's why she hid in my cellar. And only a few seconds after she found shelter in my cellar, a shell exploded in front of her house. So if she hadn't been as quick as she was, she would have died, together with her two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rendulic, this brings your testimony to an end. We thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom, and we wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. Will you allow me to say something at the end of my testimony? Which will not be part of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to thank you very much for carrying out such a responsible task. Thank you very much for everything you will do in this very responsible and important work you do for the benefit of the peace and justice in the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zivanovic, I do not blame you for any of the questions that you put to me, because I know this is your job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. The court usher will now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, once again, I would like to thank everybody, and goodbye.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll turn over the podium to my colleague Mr. Gillett for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The next witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness. Could -- can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us your name, your date of birth, and your ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tomislav Rukavina. I was born on the 6th of February, 1964, and I am Croat by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are about to make the solemn declaration, by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. That implies that you commit yourself -- your expose yourself to the penalty of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal. So can I now ask you to read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down. Mr. Gillett, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rukavina.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, did you give a statement to the Prosecution of this Tribunal in 1996?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I would ask that 65 ter 2234.1, which is an ICTY witness statement, be placed on the monitor in front of the witness. Your Honours, the Prosecution's uploaded a version of the statement with paragraph numbers added, because the previous copy did not have these, for ease of reference. And that should be tab 1A of your binder. Now, if it is agreeable to counsel, could I provide the witness with a hard copy of his statement, since I will be referring to it on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the document in front of you to be the statement that you gave in 1996 and to have your signature on it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: I do. And I -- I also recognise my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And when you gave the statement in 1996, was it read to you in your language?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And when you came to The Hague this week to testify, were you given the opportunity to read the statement and make corrections to it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, I understand you have a small number of corrections to make. Firstly, I understand that you would like to correct the spelling of the last name of the individual who's referred to as Bora Tomicic on a number of occasions in the statement. How should that name be spelt?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Boro Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Next, I understand that you'd like to correct the reference at paragraph 11, and that's pages 2 to 3 of the B/C/S copy; page 3 in the English. This is the reference to: "All of the women and children being evacuated from Bapska in the period of 2nd August to 16 August 1991." I understand that all of the women that were asked if they wanted to leave, left, but some women did not want to leave and remained in Bapska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Next, I understand that the date that is listed in your statement for when Boro Tomic came with the ultimatum from Barjaktarevic and the date when you went to the negotiations, which is listed as 27 September 1991, needs to be clarified; and at a later point in your statement, you refer to the ultimatum being read on 27 or 28 or 29 September. So my question is: What was the date on which you received the ultimatum and had negotiations with the JNA about it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: I provided my statement five years after the events so I wasn't entirely sure what date it was. That's why I hedged my answer around the 27th, 28th, or 29th. The exact date, finally, was the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And, finally, I understand that you'd like to clarify a point about the negotiations that you had with Major Barjaktarevic, and this is referred to at paragraph 17, which is page 3 of the B/C/S; page 4 of the English. There, it states that when you went for the negotiations on the border, you told him that the people in Bapska had no weapons to surrender. However, is it correct that you had hunting rifles, the people in Bapska had hunting rifles?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: That is correct. But people had permits to carry those arms, which means that those weapons were not illegal, but, rather, legal. And that's why we considered there was no need for us to hand those weapons over. They had been purchased with our own money, and they were used exclusively for sporting activities, i.e., for hunting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And did you tell Major Barjaktarevic that you had these hunting rifles?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Yes, we told him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Aside from those clarifications, is there anything else you'd like to change in the statement?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: I believe that that would be all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you affirm the accuracy and truthfulness of the information in the statement?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions about these same issues today, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Indeed, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, the Prosecution tenders the statement which is 65 ter 02234, as well as 02234.1, which is the numbered version. And they can be admitted publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think the numbered version would suffice, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Absolutely. We're happy with that being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If no objection from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P324. That's only the numbered version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rukavina, what was the ethnic composition of Bapska prior to the conflict in 1991?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Bapska was a nearly ethnically pure Croatian village. There was a very small percentage of Serbs; perhaps 1 or 2 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, looking at paragraphs 8 and 9 of your statement, which should be on page 2 to 3 in B/C/S, and page 3 in English, you refer to raids carried out by Chetniks into villages. Which villages were raided by the Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: They raided the villages that had fallen before Bapska. Dzelatovci, Nijemci, Tovarnik, Ilaca, Slakovci, Tompojevci, and the other villages that were there, including Sotin, of course. From the people who lived close to Ilok we learned the facts of those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And how close are these villages to Bapska?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: None of them were more than 20 to 25 kilometres away. They were all close to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: When the Chetniks raided these villages, how did they treat the inhabitants of the villages?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: They treated them inhumanely. There was torture, killings, rapes, and other such things. That is what we heard from the people themselves. We heard their statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And these raids that you've referred to in the various towns, when did they occur, approximately?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: On the 8th and the 9th -- or, rather, in August, September, and October. Eventually Ilok and its surroundings were raided.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And some of the villages that you referred to having fallen before Bapska, were these raids carried out before you received the ultimatum in Bapska?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Yes, before we received the ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Referring to this ultimatum which is described in your statement, you state that, at paragraph 13, Boro Tomic arrived with it. Did you see the written ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: I did. I personally received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And was it handwritten or typed?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Handwritten. And there was a signature on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And whose signature was on it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Major Slobodan Barjaktarevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Apologies. Could we get 65 ter 418.1 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do -- do you recognise the document that you see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do I understand that's the ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's the ultimatum, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, a -- a version of the ultimatum was admitted into evidence yesterday but it was somewhat difficult to read because it had been sent by fax. So we've located this version which has the same handwriting, and we would suggest that this could be linked in e-court to the already admitted version, and this way we wouldn't interfere with the already admitted version but we would have a clear version in B/C/S for the witness to read. If that's suitable to Your Honours, and if there's no objection from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If you could repeat the exhibit number, Mr. Gillett, then we will do as you ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay. The 65 ter number of the document currently on the screen is 418.1. The exhibit number of the other version that was admitted is P316.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is linked now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Rukavina, if we could look at the second paragraph of the document in front of you, just before the numbered points start -- sorry, the second paragraph before the numbered points begin.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we could zoom out a little bit. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, it states that the residents of your village of Bapska have been peaceful so far. Is that correct, that the people of Bapska had been peaceful prior to receiving this ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: They were peaceful. They did not provoke anybody, and they did not instigate anybody to do things.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what did the JNA threaten to do if you didn't comply with this ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: According to them, they would eliminate us from the face of the earth. They said that they -- that we would no longer exist on the map of the earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And would it have made a difference if you had complied with the ultimatum and handed over the weapons that you had?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think that things would have been different. If anything, they would have been worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Why would things have been worse?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Because they would have freer hands to commit the same kinds of crimes they had committed in the other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, you explain how, after receiving this ultimatum, you had negotiations with Major Slobodan Barjaktarevic and that during those negotiations, you asked whether the JNA could protect the village of Bapska. How did he respond to your proposal?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: That's correct. I asked him that. And he answered me that he did not have any such possibility, that his hands were tied.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could the JNA have protected Bapska from the Serb paramilitaries if they wanted to?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: I believe so. It was up to them whether they were willing to do that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Then why did he refuse to do so?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Most probably because they were not that well connected. There was no link between them. And let me explain. Between paramilitaries and the so-called JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Why would the lack of connection between them prevent the JNA from stopping the paramilitaries attacking Bapska?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not present. I was not one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: What weapons or arms did the JNA have?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: A range, from infantry weapons to artillery, and even planes. The whole range, the artillery included mortars, and tanks, and cannons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what weapons did the paramilitaries have?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: They mostly had light weapons, automatic rifles, Zoljas. The kind of things that they could carry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So I'm trying to understand why the JNA, with these weapons, could not have prevented the paramilitaries from attacking Bapska.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Most probably because their objective was to drive us away. They wanted to create a territory where they could be stationed and left in peace to prepare for further attacks on Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you described the ensuing attack on Bapska in your statement, and you -- you go on at paragraphs 23 and 24 of your statement to describe the evacuation of women and children to the Kordos forest after the JNA started shelling on 4 October 1991. How many women and children were in that group that were evacuated?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly. It was a large group, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Was it in the tens or the hundreds?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Several hundreds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Were any members of this group armed?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: No. There were only elderly people, women, and children in that group, and none of them were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And you state that the JNA was shelling the convoy of women and children. How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: I know because my wife was in that convoy, and she told me everything later, when we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Turning now to paragraph 25 of your statement. That is page 4 in the B/C/S; page 5 in the English. You described the tanks coming into Bapska and destroying a number of buildings. On what day did this occur?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: The attack took place on the 4th. That's when the shelling started, and they entered Bapska on the 5th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And you state that they targeted the church tower. Was this a Catholic or Orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: It was a Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we get 65 ter document 06227 placed on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you recognise this location?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: The church in Bapska. But that's not what it looked like on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what damage was done to the church when it was attacked?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: They fired at the belfry, and the bells were scattered all over the place. And a shell -- another shell hit the church itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And has it been rebuilt since then?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: You can see from this picture that it has been repaired since.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we have that -- we would tender that -- that document, 06227.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P325. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we now have document 06228 placed on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you recognise this aerial view?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's the village of Bapska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And in your statement, you describe how the JNA tanks targeted the bank. Is it possible to mark where the bank is located in Bapska?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And if the witness could please have assistance to do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can mark it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Could you mark that with an A.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we erase that and try again and put an A. Sorry, my apologies. I should have specified earlier.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we mark an A where the bank is located?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And could you please now mark a B where the church is located.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And in your statement, you mention that a number of houses and other buildings were -- were destroyed. Could you put Xs where you recall there being any buildings or houses that were destroyed, apart from the ones you've already pointed to.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And did you see those houses where you've placed Xs? Did you see that they had been destroyed or hit by weapons?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: I did. And we even tried to put out the fire on some of them. They had been torched.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender that for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number P326. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, was there a military threat to the Serb forces coming from the church?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: No, there was nothing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: What about from the bank?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Only the safe box. But I don't know whether there was anything in the safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sorry, was there a threat from the safe box, or -- why would that present a threat?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: I thought perhaps there was money in the safe, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And -- and why would that be significant, if there was money in the safe?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: It's not significant. Perhaps I thought that would be the reason why they were shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And final question on this map, was there any threat from the column of people that went to the Kordos forest that you said were shelled? Was there any threat to the JNA to -- from that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: I don't know what threat there could have been. There were only elderly people, women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, at paragraph 29 of your statement, you mention that a group of the inhabitants from Bapska left to Sid, and this was around the same time as the attack on Bapska. Why did this group of people go to Sid?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: A man, Croat, came to Bapska and said that people could leave via Sid, via Bosnia, and get to Croatia. People believed him and set out towards Sid, but they didn't go far because they ended up in the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the Prosecution goes to put some questions to the witness which are not in his statement and in summary, witness summary. And we are informed about this line -- this information last night at 8.45 -- 8 -- yes, 8.45. So I would object to this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is correct that there is information in the proofing note that has been provided, that I intend to ask the witness about it. This relates to the information in paragraph 29 of his statement, where he refers to the group of people who went to Sid and were detained in the partisan sports hall, and we wanted to inquire to what happened in these people as a follow-up to what is in his statement. And we provided notice of the information that came out in the proofing session on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, what happened to the people who were, as you say in your statement, detained in this partisan sports hall in Sid?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Some managed to get out with the help of their friends and get to Croatia via Bosnia; whereas some people were turned back to Bapska as a human shield going before military units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. This part of statement about the shield has not mentioned anywhere in the witness statement and in witness -- witness summary. And we are only informed about it from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speaker is kindly requested to generate less noise while speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- the proofing note delivered last night at 8.45. We have no time to investigate these allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, could you please read the interpreter's note in the transcript. You seem to make paper -- noise with the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I was not aware that I was so loud.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, President. If I could just add that I have already mentioned that this was a follow-up question from what is in paragraph 29 of the statement. And the Defence will almost certainly be cross-examining on Thursday, so I think they will have a bit of extra time to prepare for this. I have asked the questions that I intended to ask him about this subject. I'm not going to be delving into further detail about it. So that is the sum total of that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, turning to paragraph 31 of your statement, which is on page 5 in the B/C/S and English, you state that paramilitary troops killed four people in Bapska on 15 October. Were these victims military or civilian people?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: All of them were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You also state that the paramilitary groups burned five houses. How do you know they burned those houses?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Because some people from Bapska remained in the village, and, later, when we got to Ilok, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Later in your statement, at paragraph 35, you state that after escaping from Bapska, ten of the -- after you had escaped from Bapska, ten of the inhabitants were killed. I'm trying to understand: Were these ten people that were killed separate from the four that were killed that you mention at paragraph 31 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: That's correct. That's a separate group.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And were these people civilians or military?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Also, all of them were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: In the same paragraph, you state that 80 houses were destroyed. What ethnicity were the owners of those houses?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: All Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, aside from the specific references in paragraph 35 to killing and destruction of property, were -- after you had left or escaped from Bapska, were the inhabitants mistreated in any other ways?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: That's right. They were mistreated, abused. They were driven in the trailer of a tractor and tumbled. Their movement was restricted. They had to report every day. They were mistreated in many other ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did they have to carry out work assignments?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Some of the younger people who remained were rounded up, all of them, and taken to dig trenches for the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And where were those trenches located?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: They were taken towards a place called Lipovac, and that's where they did the digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And was this a safe activity to carry out?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Certainly not. It couldn't have been safe. Croats were ahead of you; behind you were Serbs. It -- it could not have been safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And when you say "Croats were ahead of you; behind you were Serbs," why would that make it unsafe for the people digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RUKAVINA
utterances.text: Well, if they don't kill -- get killed from one side, they can get killed from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I see we're right about the time that we're scheduled to finish and I'm about to turn to a couple of documents, so maybe we should break here, if it suits Your Honours, or I'm happy to try in the remaining 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We are at that time exactly, Mr. Gillett. Thank you. Mr. Witness, this is the end of today's hearing. Your testimony did not come to an end, so that you will have come back tomorrow morning at 9.00 -- oh, I'm sorry. Thursday, at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is it Thursday afternoon? Okay. My mistake again. It's Thursday afternoon, Mr. Witness. So I remind you that you are still on your oath. That means that you can't discuss your testimony with anybody, and you can't talk at all to any of the parties. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
